To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the availability of highly available, highly lethal methods of suicide accounts for a substantial portion (approximately one-half) of the variation in suicide mortality observed in the United States and that, in the case of firearm suicide, this variation is strongly related to differences in the distribution of household firearms across populations.

suicide mortality varies across populations more than do most other causes of death, that suicide mortality is only loosely correlated with established risk factors for suicide, that the case fatality rate for suicidal acts is strongly related to suicide mortality, that case fatality rate is strongly related to method availability, and that method availability is a key factor in explaining the variation in suicide mortality across the United States.

suicide mortality is strongly related to method availability and that the availability of highly effective suicide methods (e.g., firearms) is a major factor in the higher suicide mortality observed in rural areas and in states with higher rates of gun ownership.
